title: Bundling data with behaviour
objectives: Write a small class with an initialiser and methods.
Store data on the object with `self` and read it in methods
Give a class a readable `__repr__`, and keep mutable data per instance

screens.title: Facts that belong together
screens.prose:
A position is a few facts that belong together. This **class** bundles them.

```python
class Position:
    def __init__(self, ticker, qty, avg_price):
        self.ticker = ticker
        self.qty = qty
        self.avg_price = avg_price

shel = Position("SHEL", 150, 26.40)
azn = Position("AZN", 40, 104.20)
```

state.caption: The two objects and what each one stores

screens.question: Tap the value `azn.qty` holds.

hints.text: The name before the dot picks the object. The name after it picks the value.
This row is the object `azn`.
`azn` was made with `Position("AZN", 40, 104.20)`, so its `qty` is 40.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the row for `azn`, then the column `qty`.

byKey.r0c2: That is `shel.qty`. The name before the dot picks the object: `azn`.
byKey.r1c3: That is `azn.avg_price`. The name after the dot picks the value: `qty`.
byKey.r1c1: That is `azn.ticker`. Look one column to the right, under `qty`.

explain.text: `Position("AZN", 40, 104.20)` made a new object, an **instance** of the class. `__init__` ran and stored each argument on it, as in `self.qty = qty`. `azn.qty` reads it back: 40.

screens.prose:
A class can also carry behaviour: functions written inside it, called **methods**. This one sits inside `Position`, below `__init__`.

```python
    def value(self, price):
        return self.qty * price
```

```python
print(shel.value(27.00))
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You used the average price, £26.40. `value` multiplies by the price you pass in, £27.00.
That is the profit, $150 \times (27.00 - 26.40)$. `value` is the quantity times today's price.
You expected to pass `self` yourself. Python passes `shel` as `self`, so `27.00` lands in `price`.

hints.text: Which object is `self` in this call?
`self` is this object.
`self` is `shel`, so `self.qty` is 150. The method returns $150 \times 27.00$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out which object `self` is, then multiply.

explain.text: `shel.value(27.00)` runs `value` with `self` set to `shel` and `price` set to 27.00. So `self.qty` is 150, and the method returns $150 \times 27.00 = 4050.0$. A method's first parameter is always the object before the dot.

screens.title: Write the class
screens.prose: Now write the class yourself. Add `pnl(price)`, the profit since you bought: $q \times (p - \bar{p})$, where $\bar{p}$ is `avg_price`. A short position has a negative `qty`.
screens.question: Write `Position` with `__init__(self, ticker, qty, avg_price)`, `value(self, price)` and `pnl(self, price)`.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. Money is compared with `math.isclose`, so 90.00000000000021 counts as 90.0.

hints.text: Store each argument on the object in `__init__`, then use `self.` to read it in the methods.
A short position: `qty` is negative, so a falling price makes money.
`__init__` sets `self.ticker`, `self.qty` and `self.avg_price`. `value` returns `self.qty * price`; `pnl` returns `self.qty * (price - self.avg_price)`.

feedback.correct: SHEL shows £90.00 profit, AZN a £108.00 loss, and the BARC short a £25.00 profit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 reads `.ticker`. An `AttributeError` means `__init__` did not store it: write `self.ticker = ticker`.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 expects 90.0 for SHEL bought at £26.40 and now £27.00. Subtract the average price from today's price.

explain.text: Every method reaches the stored facts through `self`. The BARC short gains as the price falls: $-500 \times (1.80 - 1.85) = 25.0$. The same formula works for long and short positions.

screens.prose:
You print a position to check it.

```python
print(shel)
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: Python cannot guess how you want your object shown. By default it prints the class name and a memory address.
An object is not a dict. By default Python shows only its class and where it lives in memory.

hints.text: Has the class told Python how to show a `Position` as text?
Python knows these values, but not how you want them shown.
With no instructions, Python prints the class name and a memory address.

feedback.correct: Without instructions, Python shows the class and an address.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The class has not said how to show itself.

explain.text: Python asks an object for its text by calling its `__repr__` method. The default one shows the class and a memory address. Define your own `__repr__` and `print`, the console and lists all use it.

screens.prose: Give `Position` a readable `__repr__`. It must **return** a string, not print one. Format the price with `{self.avg_price:.2f}` so it keeps two places.
screens.question: Add `__repr__` so that `repr(Position("SHEL", 150, 26.4))` is `Position(SHEL, 150 @ £26.40)`.

widget.how: Check runs 4 hidden tests. Test 4 shows a list of positions, which uses `__repr__` for each one.

hints.text: An f-string builds the text. `return` hands it back.
`return f"Position({self.ticker}, {self.qty} @ £{self.avg_price:.2f})"`

feedback.correct: Positions now show themselves, alone and inside lists.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects `'Position(SHEL, 150 @ £26.40)'`. `£26.4` means the `:.2f` is missing. A `TypeError` about a non-string means you printed instead of returning.

explain.text: `__repr__` returns the text Python shows for the object. `:.2f` keeps two decimal places, as prices need. `str()` falls back to `__repr__` and lists always use it, so one method covers every display.

screens.prose:
A colleague writes `__init__` without `self.`:

```python
class Position:
    def __init__(self, ticker, qty, avg_price):
        ticker = ticker
        qty = qty
        avg_price = avg_price

shel = Position("SHEL", 150, 26.40)
print(shel.qty)
```
screens.question: What happens?

options.why: You expected `qty = qty` to store the value on the object. Without `self.` it only sets a local name, gone when `__init__` ends.
Python does not fill missing attributes with `None`. Reading one that was never set raises an error.
`shel.qty` asks the object for an attribute, so a failure is an `AttributeError`, not a `NameError`.

hints.text: Which of these lines puts anything on the object `self`?
These are local names. They vanish when `__init__` returns.
`qty = qty` reassigns a local name to itself. Nothing is stored on `self`, so `shel.qty` does not exist.

feedback.correct: Nothing was stored on the object, so `shel.qty` does not exist.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what `qty = qty` changes.

byKey.stored: You expected `qty = qty` to store 150 on the object. It only reassigns a local name, which disappears when `__init__` returns.
byKey.none: You expected a missing attribute to read as `None`. Python raises `AttributeError` instead.
byKey.name: The lookup is on the object, `shel.qty`, so the error is `AttributeError`.

explain.text: Inside `__init__`, `qty` is just a local name, like any parameter. Only `self.qty = qty` attaches the value to the object, where it outlives the call. Every attribute you want to keep needs `self.`.

canvas.caption: Only self survives the call; the local names vanish

screens.prose:
A first try at a trading book keeps its list in the class body.

```python
class Book:
    trades = []

    def add(self, trade):
        self.trades.append(trade)

mine = Book()
yours = Book()
mine.add("VOD +100")
print(len(yours.trades))
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You expected each book to get its own list. `trades = []` runs once, when the class is made, so every book shares that one list.
`yours` has no `trades` of its own, so Python looks in the class and finds the shared list there.

hints.text: How many times does the line `trades = []` run?
Neither book stores a list of its own. Both look it up in the class.
One list lives on the class. `mine.add` appends to it, and `yours.trades` is the same list, so its length is 1.

feedback.correct: Both books share the one list in the class.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many lists exist.

explain.text: `trades = []` in the class body runs once, so there is one list on the class. `self.trades` finds it through the class for every book. Write `self.trades = []` inside `__init__` and each book gets its own list.

canvas.caption: One list, reached by both books

screens.prose:
You have seen what a method call does. Python passes the object before the dot as the first argument:

$$\texttt{shel.value(27.00)} \;=\; \texttt{Position.value(shel, 27.00)}$$

So every method starts with `self`, and data stored as `self.name` lives on that one object.
screens.question: Which call is the same as `azn.pnl(101.50)`?

options.why: That leaves out the object. `101.50` would land in `self`, and `price` would be missing.
`pnl` lives inside the class. There is no plain name `pnl` outside it.

feedback.correct: The object before the dot becomes `self`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the object in as the first argument.

explain.text: `azn.pnl(101.50)` becomes `Position.pnl(azn, 101.50)`, so `self` is `azn` and `price` is 101.50. It returns $40 \times (101.50 - 104.20) = -108.0$.

screens.title: A trading book
screens.prose: A trading book records fills and nets them by ticker. Buys have positive `qty`, sells negative. The type hints document what each method takes and returns.
screens.question: Complete `Trade` and `Book`. `net(ticker)` is the total quantity for that ticker (0 if none). `cash()` is the cash flow, $-\sum q \times p$, rounded to 2 places.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. Each builds a fresh `Book`, adds trades, then reads the last value. Test 2 checks that two books do not share trades.

hints.text: Give each `Book` its own list in `__init__`. `add` appends to it.
These two VOD fills net to 600 shares.
`net` adds `t.qty` for each trade whose `t.ticker` matches. `cash` adds `t.qty * t.price` over all trades and returns `round(-total, 2)`.

feedback.correct: VOD nets to 600 shares, and the book paid out £420.00 net.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 adds AZN to one book and asks another. A list written in the class body is shared; create it in `__init__` with `self.trades = []`.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 asks for BARC, which this book never traded, and expects 0. Count only the trades whose `ticker` matches.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 expects −420.0: buying spends cash, so the sign is negative. Return `round(-total, 2)`.

explain.text: Buying 1,000 VOD at £0.72 spends £720.00, and selling 400 at £0.75 brings back £300.00. So `net("VOD")` is 600 and `cash()` is −420.0. Each book keeps its own list because `__init__` makes a new one.

ideas: A class bundles data with the functions that use it. `__init__` stores each value on the new object as `self.name`.
`obj.method(x)` runs `Class.method(obj, x)`: the object before the dot arrives as `self`. `__repr__` decides how the object prints.
Create lists in `__init__`. A list written in the class body is shared by every instance.

formula.name: A method call
formula.note: So `def value(self, price):` needs `self` first, and `self.qty` reads this object's quantity.

summary.trap: `qty = qty` inside `__init__` stores nothing on the object. Write `self.qty = qty`.

quiz.question: What happens?

options.text: A `TypeError`: `value` gets one argument too many

options.why: The method has no `self` parameter. Python still passes the object, so two arguments arrive for one slot.
The call fails before the body runs. Python passes two arguments to a method that accepts one.

feedback.correct: The object arrives as an extra argument, and `value` has no slot for it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the arguments Python passes to `value`.

explain.text: `Position(10).value(5.00)` passes the object and 5.00, but `value(price)` takes one argument. Write `def value(self, price):`.

quiz.prose:
```python
a = Position("VOD", 100, 0.72)
b = a
b.qty = 300
print(a.qty)
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: You expected `b = a` to copy the position. It gives the same object a second name, so changing `b.qty` changes `a.qty`.
`b` is the same object as `a`, and it has a `qty`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Does `b = a` make a new object?

explain.text: `b = a` copies no data: both names point at the one `Position`. Setting `b.qty` changes that object, so `a.qty` is 300.

quiz.prose:
```python
class Order:
    tags = []

    def __init__(self, tag):
        self.tags.append(tag)

first = Order("urgent")
second = Order("small")
print(first.tags)
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: You expected each order to have its own list. `tags = []` sits in the class body, so both orders append to one shared list.
`__init__` appends each tag. Both appends land in the class's single list.

feedback.correct: One list on the class, shared by both orders.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many `tags` lists exist?

explain.text: The class body runs once, so there is one `tags` list. Each `__init__` appends to it. Create the list with `self.tags = [tag]` inside `__init__`.

quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: The list shows each item's `__repr__` text as it is. The quotes appear only when the items are strings.
The class defines `__repr__`, and lists use it for every item.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does a list use to show its items?

explain.text: A list shows each item with `__repr__`. Here that returns `VOD x100` and `AZN x40`, placed inside the brackets as they are.
